 Nicola Coughlan Says She Would Never Be in HBO’s Harry Potter Show and Won’t Watch It
 The trans ally made it absolutely clear where she stands.
 By Mathew Rodriguez , November 16, 2026 When it comes to HBO’s new Harry Potter series, it’s a hard no from Nicola Coughlan. 
 The Bridgerton actress said that fans shouldn’t expect her to appear in the series-length retelling of J.K. Rowling’s fantasy novels, the first season of which is set to debut on HBO on Christmas Day of this year. Despite being a huge fan of the books when she was younger, the series is not her cup of butterbeer anymore. 
 “I will not be watching the new Harry Potter show and I would never be in it,” she told British outlet The Observer in a profile published Friday. “Look, I know people that are involved in those shows, and they’re nice people and whatever, but it’s not for me.”
 While it might seem unusual for an actor to turn down work, Coughlan has been a vocal supporter of transgender rights, which many people see as being at odds with supporting HBO’s Harry Potter and, by extension, Rowling. In the last six years, the author has used her cultural prominence and parts of her vast fortune to advocate against equality for trans people; she also serves as an executive producer on the TV reboot.
 In 2025, Coughlan slammed the U.K. Supreme Court’s decision to define legal sex by a person’s assigned gender at birth. 
 “I feel like the rights of queer people have been chipped away for the last few years, and this is a blatant move to take rights away from people,” she said at the time. “The ruling means trans women won’t be able to use the women’s bathroom, and the idea of trans women attacking women in bathrooms. The only time I have ever been made to feel scared has been by cis men. I have never been scared by a trans woman in my life.”
 Immediately following the 2025 court ruling, she raised £70,000 (roughly $96,000) for trans U.K. charity Not a Phase. 
 “To see an already marginalized community… be further attacked in law is really stomach turning and disgusting, and these people celebrating it [are] more stomach turning and disgusting,” Coughlan said in a video at the time. “If you are a cisgender person who is an ally of a trans person, I think now is the time to just… speak up and make your voice heard, and let your trans, nonbinary friends and just the community at large know that you’re there for them and will keep fighting for them.”
 Since the announcement of the cast and creative team behind the new Harry Potter series, many actors and creatives have been vocal about whether they would be attached to the project, given Rowling’s views and political activity through her J.K. Rowling Women’s Fund. 
 Out queer directors Ally Pankiw and Kate Herron publicly said in August that they turned down working on the series. Both directors offered public comment after actor Nicholas Hoult announced that he would join the series as Gilderoy Lockhart in its already greenlit second season. Hoult dropped out less than two weeks later following fan backlash, citing scheduling conflicts, and was replaced by Game of Thrones actor Kit Harrington . 
 In recent months, actors involved with the show have been vocal in interviews about their support for transgender people. In August, Bel Powley, who will play Petunia Dursley, said she “strongly disagrees” with the views of the series’ author. Earlier this month, Papaa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, declined to comment directly on Rowling, but did say that he supported trans people.
 “I don’t want to talk about Jo at all,” he told Vanity Fair . He continued, “I believe, in my bones, that trans people, queer people, people of all creeds and color have got the right to be treated with respect and dignity and safety at all times — whether they’re in the workplace, whether they’re at home or in the street, whatever.” He added, “That’s what I believe, and that’s the way that I choose to live my life. That’s the creed by which I live.”
 In the new profile, Coughlan told the Observer that she believes celebrities should use their platforms for social change.
 “In reality, people actually can help and make a difference,” she said. “Six million followers is loads. But people have hundreds of millions. If you had 20 million, how much money could you raise?”
 She also said she was disappointed in celebrities who don’t speak out. 
 “I had interesting conversations with certain people who said to me, ‘I’m not in a strong enough position,’ or ‘I don’t get to say anything, because my career is not as good’, or ‘I have too much to lose.’ And I thought, this is bullshit, isn’t it?,” she said. “Everyone has something to lose and everyone has something to gain.” 
 She added, “I just think I would never forgive myself if I didn’t say, ‘I think this is really fucking wrong,’ and I have a platform, and I want to try and do something practical, and that’s to raise money.”
 The Observer also questioned Coughlan about Rowling’s 2025 response to the U.K. Supreme Court’s decision, in which she took a dig at both Coughlan and Pedro Pascal by saying, “Who are they?” Both actors had previously taken a swipe at the author’s transphobic bullying .
 “Me, I could believe,” Coughlan told the Observer . “But Pedro Pascal? You know who Pedro Pascal is, girl. Like, please.”
 Coughlan’s comments come just as the series released the first full clip from the upcoming series, which was roundly lambasted online for its poor CGI, color grading, and overall lifelessness .
